source.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y) = x^2y^2+\sin{x}\cos{y},$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ at the point $(\pi,2\pi).$
source.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot (2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡y\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =2x{y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\pi,2\pi)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(\pi ,2\pi )} & =2\cdot \pi \cdot (2\pi )^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi  \\  & =2\pi \cdot 4{\pi }^{2}+(-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =8{\pi }^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$
